headline: Scottsdale Grandfather Survives Diamondback Strike on Evening Walk; SnakeNews Safety Desk Sounds the Rattle
summary: An Arizona man is recovering after stepping on a rattlesnake in his Scottsdale neighborhood, and SnakeNews has the safety tips every Santa Monica walker needs to hear.
body:
I'm Philip Massouh, and this is SnakeNews. Tonight, a 66-year-old grandfather in Scottsdale, Arizona, is counting himself very blessed and very fortunate after a diamondback rattlesnake struck him during an evening walk in his own neighborhood. Because if there is one thing SnakeNews knows, it is that snakes are not just out on remote hiking trails. They are under decks. They are inside sheds. They are coiled in outdoor equipment. And sometimes, they are exactly where your left foot is about to land.

The man, Gary Takacs, was walking near his home after dark when he accidentally stepped on a diamondback rattlesnake. He said it happened in an instant. He put his left foot down and the snake bit his ankle. He was wearing running shoes and short socks, no hiking boots and no ankle protection. He described the feeling as a charge of electricity running through his leg. In his words, 'Extreme pain, felt the fangs, could feel it and then instantly felt the pain from the bite.'

Somehow, he was able to walk a few blocks back to his house. His wife called 911. Takacs was given a dose of anti-venom and spent the night in a hospital intensive care unit. He is expected to make a full recovery. He is a frequent runner and hiker, and he says he is giving his grandkids stories to tell. He told the outlet, 'I just count myself very blessed, very fortunate.' Now he wants other people to know that this time of year requires extra precautions and a sharp eye for rattlesnakes.

Here is the part that should make you sit up straight. Aries Clark with the Phoenix Herpetological Sanctuary said that when the weather heats up, rattlesnakes can pop up anywhere, not just on hiking trails. Clark removed a snake from a neighborhood garage just the other day. That means this is not a wilderness problem. It is a driveway problem, a patio problem, a shed problem. The diamondback rattlesnake is found in a majority of the United States and is more common in the southwest. Experts say they are most likely to be found near water in the early morning or late evening.

That brings us to the SnakeNews Safety Desk. I am joined by our own Chip Morales, and Chip has the kind of advice that can save your leg. Chip says, first, call 911 immediately. Stay calm. Keep the bitten limb still and at or below the level of your heart. Do not apply a tourniquet. Do not cut the wound. Do not try to suck out the venom. Do not pack it in ice. Do not chase the snake to identify it. The antivenom does the work, and the professionals need you to get to the hospital as safely as possible.

The experts are also clear about prevention. If you see or hear a rattler, step away very slowly. Do not poke it. Do not test its patience. Snakes generally avoid confrontation and usually only strike if provoked. The best way to know if a snake is venomous is to learn the specific species in your area, including their patterns, markings, and preferred habitat. Head shape and eye shape are not a one hundred percent reliable way to tell, and if you are close enough to check, you are too close. Wear closed-toed shoes when you are walking in wooded areas or working in your garden. Keep grass trimmed low. Be cautious around wood piles and leaf piles. And if you find a snake on your property, have a professional remove it. In some states, it is illegal to kill snakes.

Time now for our Santa Monica check-in. I know what you are all wondering. Philip, are you okay? Yes. I am fine. I checked my front porch, my back deck, and the little strip of succulents by the mailbox. No rattlesnake under the barbecue cover, no coil by the hose reel, no sudden fang marks on my ankles. I am safe, I am alert, and I am wearing the tallest socks I own. But I am also taking the Scottsdale lesson to heart. If a snake can find a garage in Phoenix, it can find a garden in Santa Monica. So I am carrying a light, watching where I step, and backing away very slowly from anything that rattles.

That is the real story tonight. Gary Takacs went for a walk in his own neighborhood and ended up in an ICU with a diamondback rattlesnake bite. He is going to recover, and he wants you to be more aware. He says he will use a head lamp from now on, because being up before sunrise or after sunset means you need to see exactly where your feet are going. So do it. Watch your step. Give snakes space. Call 911 if you are bitten, and do not try to be a hero with a knife or a tourniquet. I'm Philip Massouh, and this is SnakeNews. Stay safe, stay rattled in the right way, and for the love of everything, watch your ankles.
